answers.answer: The client sends a request to the balancer, which selects and forwards to an application backend; the backend performs the work and sends its response through the balancer to the client. Choose L7 for /search and /purchase pools: it needs readable HTTP contents, normally terminating client TLS for HTTPS; backend encryption is a separate choice. L4 typically selects per TCP connection, so many requests reusing that connection can all reach the same backend without new selections. A single adequate server may suffice when neither traffic distribution nor redundant serving is needed.

evidence.quote: In a reverse-proxy arrangement, the client contacts one service entry point. The balancer forwards the request to a selected backend, which performs the operation and returns a response through the balancer to the client.

Understands HTTP requests. It can route /images and /reports to different backend groups, or select a backend for each request. Rules that keep a user on one backend can override independent selection.

Path routing requires readable HTTP contents. TLS encrypts the connection; an HTTPS proxy normally ends, or terminates, that TLS connection to inspect requests. Encryption to the backend is a separate configuration choice.
Many HTTP requests can reuse that connection. They can all reach the same backend; adding requests on that connection does not force new selections.
One adequate server may be enough if the service does not need traffic distribution or redundant serving.

answers.answer: Round robin takes turns across eligible backends, counting a cheap lookup and a long request equally, so equal turns need not balance work. Least connections prefers fewer active connections and can help with long uneven work, but connection count hides different work per connection. Weights control traffic share; twice measured capacity suggests an initial twice weight, but configuration is neither live measurement nor a performance guarantee. Verify latency and resource use. Another API backend alone does not remove a saturated shared database bottleneck. Availability requires a reachable alternate entry path with tested failover if a lone balancer fails, plus enough spare capacity on surviving backends; limit or visibly reject excess work if survivors cannot carry it.

evidence.quote: Takes turns across eligible backends. It is a simple starting point for similar servers and similar work; a quick read and a slow report still each count as one request.
Prefers the backend with fewer active connections. This can help when connection durations vary, but one connection may carry far more work than another.
Bias the share of traffic. A server with twice the measured capacity might start with twice the weight. Configured weights are not a live measurement or a performance guarantee.
For long, uneven work, consider least connections; for unequal server capacity, consider weights. Check actual latency and resource use before deciding: no policy is universally best.
Balancing distributes existing capacity. More API servers can help when API processing is the bottleneck; they do not remove a saturated shared database bottleneck.

Headroom is spare capacity. After one backend fails, the survivors need enough capacity for the remaining load. Otherwise redirecting traffic can overload them. Limit or reject excess work visibly instead of assuming redistribution solves it.

A lone balancer is itself a possible failure point. If it fails, clients need a reachable alternate entry path, not just another disconnected balancer box. Use an available managed entry or redundant frontends with working failover, and test that path.

answers.answer: A 200 health response only shows the sampled endpoint works; purchase readiness requires the database capability needed for useful work. Use a check reflecting that capability. Even then, limited coverage, periodic intervals and failure thresholds delay detection, and failure can occur just after a pass. Once detected and removed, the backend receives no new selections, but removal cannot complete, undo or safely replay underway requests, which can still fail. Check the product all-unhealthy policy, since some still send traffic to unhealthy targets when every check fails.

evidence.quote: A health check periodically probes a backend. Readiness means it can accept useful new work: a process can answer /health while an application handler cannot reach its required database.

Use a check that reflects the capabilities needed to serve application requests. Checks have limited coverage, intervals and failure thresholds; a backend can fail just after passing. Detection takes time.
Once detected and removed from eligible backends, it stops receiving new selections. Requests already underway can still fail; removal does not complete, undo or safely replay them.
Check the product's all-unhealthy policy too. Some balancers send traffic to unhealthy targets when every target fails its checks, rather than refusing all traffic.

answers.answer: B cannot read a cart held only in A memory; losing A can lose its only copy. Stickiness prefers A for ordinary requests, but can skew load and restrict placement. It neither copies the cart nor preserves it on A failure. Shared session storage lets either backend read the cart, at the cost of access or coordination work and a shared dependency whose availability also matters.

evidence.quote: Session state is information kept between a user's requests. If a server keeps a user's session only in A's memory, B cannot read it. Losing A can lose the only copy.
Prefers the same backend for that user's requests. It can keep ordinary requests on A, but skew load and restrict placement. It does not copy the session or preserve it when A fails.
Lets either backend read the session. It adds access or coordination work and a shared dependency whose availability matters too.

answers.answer: First stop new assignments to A, handle existing connection lifetimes or stop accepting further requests, and track already accepted work. Let the accepted 20-second request finish within a bounded drain deadline, then shut A down after completion or at expiry. The deadline value is unspecified, so completion is not guaranteed; forced termination may interrupt unfinished work and does not automatically move it to B. Stopping only new L4 connections still allows HTTP requests on the reused connection. Drain behavior must therefore address connection lifetimes for L4 and accepted requests for L7, not merely new connections.

evidence.quote: During a deployment, draining stops new assignments to A while allowing in-flight work, meaning requests already underway, to finish within a deadline. Shut A down after completion or when that deadline expires.

Stopping new L4 connections does not stop new HTTP requests on existing connections. A drain must also manage those connection lifetimes or stop accepting further requests. L7 request-aware draining must still track already accepted work.
Give a running request time to finish, but bound the wait. Forced termination at the deadline may interrupt unfinished requests. Their work is not automatically moved to B.

answers.answer: Although the question says A committed, the lost response gives the client no confirmation; retrying blindly at B can apply the purchase again. Reuse one stable idempotency key for the logical purchase on every attempt. All backends consult a shared durable key/result record: in one database transaction uniquely reserve the key, apply the purchase effect and record the result, committing all or none. A repeat returns the recorded result without another effect. Separate check-then-write can race or leave a crash gap. A fresh retry key fails to identify the same operation, and A-only memory cannot reliably protect a retry on B. Limit and delay retries because they consume capacity and can worsen overload; retries do not guarantee success or replace duplicate protection.

evidence.quote: A backend commits a write, but its response is lost. The client cannot tell whether the write completed. A blind retry on another backend can repeat the effect.

A stable ID for one logical operation, reused on every attempt. Deduplication means recognizing a repeat. A new key per retry, or a key remembered only in one server's memory, cannot reliably protect retries elsewhere.

All backends use a shared durable record of the key and result. In one database transaction, reserve the key uniquely, apply the effect and record the result; commit all or none. A repeat returns the recorded result without applying the effect again. Separate check-then-write steps can race or leave a crash gap.
Bound retry attempts and delay them: extra requests consume capacity and can deepen overload. Retry policy does not replace duplicate protection or guarantee success.
